title: E.D.S.O.
hook: The leaderboard is bright, the room is fast, and nobody is helping the slow station.
counterintuition: The trap is not low motivation. It is overfeeding quick individual rewards until trust-building rewards feel slow, optional, or invisible.
tryThisNow: Look at one scoreboard or incentive and mark whether it rewards chase, status, bonding, or care. Change one signal that crowds out trust.
keyTakeaway: Culture changes when leaders rebalance the reward pattern, so quick wins do not starve the slower rewards that build trust.

breakdown.fastRead:
A cafe tip crown can make the room faster and meaner at the same time. The winning barista chases the visible prize while the backed-up milk station falls behind. The system is not neutral. It is teaching people what feels worth doing.

E.D.S.O. gives leaders a way to read group rewards. Some rewards feel quick and solo. Others grow through care, trust, and shared credit. A healthy culture feeds both, not just the quick hit.
breakdown.deepRead:
A scoreboard can change a room before anyone changes a value statement. If the board rewards only fast case counts, merged code, personal splits, or daily tips, people learn where the good feeling lives. They may work harder. They may also stop teaching, reviewing, pacing, or helping when those acts do not count.

Use the chemical language lightly. Endorphins and dopamine are useful shorthand for relief, chase, and completion. Serotonin and oxytocin point toward status, trust, bonding, and care. The point is not to pretend a leader can manage brains like switches. The point is to notice what the system makes easiest to crave. If all the visible rewards belong to the quick win, then the slower social rewards get treated as nice but secondary.

Stimulation is not the same as culture.

The leadership move is to audit the reward pattern. What gets applause? What gets counted? What gets named in public? What helps a person feel proud because someone else succeeded? A radiology room can keep case counts and add shared credit for difficult peer review. A volunteer desk can honor handoffs that made another volunteer succeed. The quick win stays, but it no longer owns the room.
breakdown.fullRead:
A group can be highly motivated and still become less trustworthy. That is the warning inside this lens. People may move faster, clear more tickets, win more points, or collect more visible praise while the habits that hold the group together quietly lose value. Help becomes inefficient. Teaching becomes charity. Review becomes a tax on personal output. Care becomes invisible labor.

You can see it when a cafe crowns the solo tip winner while the milk station drowns. You can see it in a release cycle where easy merges earn status and hard review work disappears. You can see it in a rowing club where athletes chase personal splits and hide fatigue because boat-average recovery is not on the board. The reward pattern has started to train self-protection under the cover of achievement.

A brief aside: E.D.S.O. is best used as a map, not a lab report. Endorphins, dopamine, serotonin, and oxytocin give names to familiar pulls. Relief after effort. The chase of a visible goal. The status of being valued. The bond that grows when help is safe and returned. A leader does not need to overexplain the chemistry to use the distinction. The practical question is simpler: what kind of reward does this place make easy, and what kind does it make invisible?

That question changes incentives. The chief radiologist does not abolish case targets. He pairs them with peer-review blocks where difficult reads earn shared credit. The open-source maintainer does not stop counting merged code. She tags unseen review work in the release notes before the merge count. The chess organizer does not end the ladder. He gives ladder credit for annotated games with new players. The system still rewards effort, but it also rewards trust-building behavior.

There is a limit. Some quick rewards are good. People need progress, completion, competition, relief, and visible wins. A culture without any quick reward can become vague and flat. The failure is letting one reward type dominate until people learn that the fastest private hit is the safest path.

When leaders rebalance the pattern, cooperation becomes less heroic. A person can help the slow station without losing all status. A senior contributor can review hard work without disappearing from the release story. A strong rower can pace the boat and still feel recognized. The room learns a different kind of satisfaction: not just I won, but we got stronger because I used my strength where it helped the group.

examples.title: Megan Erases the Tip Crown

planSpec.stakes: baristas chase tips and stop helping the slow station
planSpec.requiredBeat: she removes the solo tip crown and posts a shared recovery score for rush periods

examples.scenario: A chalk leaderboard leans beside a backed-up milk pitcher while the morning line curls to the door. Megan sees the top-tip crown circled twice, and the winning barista is staying on register instead of helping steam milk. Before lunch, she must decide whether the board rewards service or only the quick solo hit.
examples.whatToDo: Remove the solo tip crown and post a shared rush recovery score that includes handoffs to the slow station. Keep tips visible, but stop crowning isolation.
examples.whyItMatters: The old board made the fastest private reward easiest to chase. Megan adds a reward for trust-building help when the room is under pressure.

examples.title: Anton Adds Shared Credit

planSpec.stakes: fast case counts reduce teaching and trust
planSpec.requiredBeat: he pairs the case counter with a peer-review block where difficult reads earn shared credit

examples.scenario: "Thirty reads by noon," someone says as a grayscale scan freezes on the diagnostic monitor. Anton watches a difficult case slide into the peer-review queue untouched. The case counter is working, but teaching is fading. He is about to decide whether to keep rewarding speed alone or pair the counter with shared credit for hard reads.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the case counter, but add a peer-review block where difficult reads earn shared credit for the first reader and reviewer. Make teaching count in the same room as speed.
examples.whyItMatters: Anton does not remove achievement. He prevents the quick count from starving the social reward of being trusted, helped, and recognized for careful judgment.

examples.title: Beatrice Changes the Erg Board

planSpec.stakes: athletes hide fatigue and stop pacing teammates
planSpec.requiredBeat: the coach asks which boat wins if the fastest rower burns out, then changes the board to boat-average recovery

examples.scenario: The erg screen flashes a split time while flywheels hiss in the winter room. Beatrice points to the boat roster and asks, "Which boat wins if the fastest rower burns out by February?" Everyone predicts the top split will stay posted. Before the next test, she must decide whether to reward the solo spike or boat-average recovery.
examples.whatToDo: Change the board from best personal split only to boat-average recovery after hard pieces. Praise pacing that keeps the whole crew strong.
examples.whyItMatters: The reveal shifts reward from personal chase to shared durability. Athletes can still push hard without hiding fatigue from the boat.

examples.title: Lin Names the Review Work

planSpec.stakes: contributors choose easy fixes over hard reviews
planSpec.requiredBeat: the maintainer tags unseen review work in the release notes before counting merged code

examples.scenario: Lin noticed the release getting thinner when the review queue stayed full and tiny fixes kept landing. The pull-request queue was filtered by review needed, but the release notes counted only merged code. Before posting the next release, Lin tagged unseen review work by name, then listed merged changes beneath it. On this open source release triage assignment, Lin is the lead others will follow.
examples.whatToDo: Put hard review work in the release notes before the merge count. Name the contributors who made risky patches safer even when they did not add new code.
examples.whyItMatters: The old count rewarded easy completion. Lin adds status for care and trust, so contributors do not have to choose between helping and being seen.

examples.title: Clara Starts the Gratitude Log

planSpec.stakes: volunteers hoard visible shifts and avoid quiet patient support
planSpec.requiredBeat: she creates a gratitude log for handoffs that made another volunteer succeed

examples.scenario: Which volunteer gets seen: the one wearing visitor badges at the front desk or the one who quietly sets up the next shift? Clara stands by the badge printer beside a blank gratitude log. Last month she ranked hours served. This month she asks volunteers to record handoffs that made someone else's shift succeed.
examples.whatToDo: Keep tracking hours, but add a gratitude log for handoffs, patient support, and quiet setup that helped another volunteer succeed.
examples.whyItMatters: Clara makes care visible. The reward pattern shifts from hoarding public shifts toward building the trust that lets volunteers rely on each other.

examples.title: Diego Credits the Practice Game

planSpec.stakes: players chase rating points and stop teaching beginners
planSpec.requiredBeat: he offers ladder credit for annotated practice games with new players

examples.scenario: You sit across from Diego while a chess clock ticks beside an annotation notebook. "Why teach beginners if ladder points only come from wins?" a player asks. Diego turns the notebook around. "Annotated practice games will count too." Before the next pairing, he must decide whether the ladder rewards status alone or shared growth. For this city chess club ladder case, Diego is the lead close enough to act.
examples.whatToDo: Offer ladder credit for annotated practice games with new players. Require useful notes, not easy wins, and post them beside rating gains.
examples.whyItMatters: Diego keeps competition but adds reward for teaching. Strong players can earn status by helping others improve, not only by taking points.

questions.prompt: A support team leaderboard ranks only tickets closed per hour. Senior agents stop helping new hires because coaching lowers their rank. Which change best rebalances the reward pattern?
choices: Add shared credit for coached tickets that stay resolved after review.
Remove all tracking so no one feels pressure.
Raise the closure target so agents work harder.
questions.explanation: Shared credit keeps achievement while rewarding trust-building help. Removing tracking drops useful feedback, while a higher target worsens the solo chase.

questions.prompt: A manager says morale is high because employees compete hard for daily badges. Yet peer review is ignored and people hide mistakes. What is the best reading of the system?
choices: The badges prove culture is healthy because energy is high.
The system may be stimulating people while starving trust rewards.
Peer review should be optional because competition is working.
questions.explanation: Energy is not enough. The badges may overfeed quick individual reward while making slower cooperation feel unrewarded.

questions.prompt: A newsroom celebrates reporters with the most bylines, and editors notice fewer people helping with fact checks on hard stories. Which incentive would best add social reward?
choices: Give the top byline reporter a larger solo prize.
Stop publishing bylines for every story.
Credit fact-check partners in the story notes and monthly review.
questions.explanation: Crediting fact-check partners gives status to care that protects the group. Bigger solo prizes increase the quick hit, and no bylines may erase useful recognition.

questions.prompt: A coach wants athletes to pursue personal records without hiding fatigue from teammates. Which scoreboard design best fits the E.D.S.O. lens?
choices: Track personal records and add a team recovery score that rewards pacing and honest fatigue reporting.
Track only the fastest personal record each week.
Ban personal records because competition harms trust.
questions.explanation: The first design keeps quick achievement and adds a trust reward. The other choices either overfeed the solo chase or remove useful drive.

questions.prompt: A hospital unit recognizes volunteers only by hours served. Volunteers begin choosing visible desk shifts and avoiding quiet patient escorts. What should the coordinator audit first?
choices: Which volunteers are least committed to service.
Whether the recognition system makes care work invisible.
How to make desk shifts harder to get.
questions.explanation: The issue is the reward signal, not first a character flaw. If patient escort work is invisible, the system trains people away from it.

questions.prompt: A product team gives a loud prize for most features shipped. Engineers start avoiding maintenance work that prevents outages. Which move best avoids confusing stimulation with culture?
choices: Keep the feature prize and add visible credit for maintenance that reduces risk.
Tell engineers maintenance is part of the job and should need no credit.
Cancel all prizes and hope people choose wisely.
questions.explanation: Adding credit for maintenance makes care visible beside speed. Saying it should need no credit ignores the actual signal the system sends.

questions.prompt: A teacher awards points for fastest correct answers. Students stop explaining methods to classmates. Which reward pattern is likely being overfed?
choices: A quick individual completion reward that crowds out shared learning.
A trust-building reward that makes students too slow.
A care reward that removes achievement.
questions.explanation: Fast-answer points reward the quick solo hit. The missing behavior is shared explanation, which needs recognition if it matters.

questions.prompt: An open-source maintainer notices contributors choosing typo fixes over careful reviews because merge counts are public. Which action best changes the culture signal?
choices: Hide all contribution records from the project.
Publish review credits and difficult-review notes before the merge count.
Tell contributors that mature people should not need recognition.
questions.explanation: Publishing review credit makes unseen trust work visible. Hiding everything removes useful signal, and scolding ignores the reward pattern already in place.

questions.prompt: A sales floor feels lively because reps ring a bell for every deal, but nobody helps with complex renewals that protect long-term clients. What should the leader add?
choices: A louder bell for the largest solo deal.
Recognition for shared saves on complex renewals, named with the people who helped.
A rule banning celebration after any sale.
questions.explanation: Shared renewal recognition rewards trust and care without denying achievement. A louder solo bell deepens the imbalance, while banning celebration throws out useful energy.

reviewCards.front: A scoreboard makes people faster but less helpful. What should you audit?
reviewCards.back: Audit the reward pattern: what gets counted, praised, and named. Look for quick individual rewards crowding out trust-building work.

reviewCards.front: How should leaders use E.D.S.O. without overclaiming chemistry?
reviewCards.back: Use it as a practical map of reward types, not a lab manual. Ask what the system makes easy to crave and what it makes invisible.

reviewCards.front: What is the danger of quick hits dominating a culture?
reviewCards.back: People can stay energized while becoming less willing to teach, review, help, or care when those acts cost personal reward.

reviewCards.front: A leader wants both achievement and trust. What should incentives do?
reviewCards.back: Keep useful achievement rewards and add visible credit for behavior that makes others safer, stronger, or more able to succeed.

reviewCards.front: Why is stimulation not the same as culture?
reviewCards.back: A room can feel busy and exciting while its reward pattern teaches people to chase private wins instead of shared strength.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice reading incentives as emotional training. Keep useful quick wins, but add visible rewards for trust, care, review, teaching, and shared success.

ifThenPlans.plan: If I review a leaderboard, then I will name one cooperative behavior it ignores and add a way for that behavior to be seen.
If I create a contest, then I will pair the individual win with one shared measure that protects help and honesty.
If I praise a visible result, then I will also name the unseen handoff, review, or care that made the result safer.
If people stop helping under pressure, then I will inspect what the current reward pattern makes them lose when they help.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Find one metric, prize, or public praise habit. Add one sentence or field that gives credit to a trust-building behavior it currently ignores.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, choose one visible win and trace the hidden care and forces behind it. Publicly credit that care before celebrating the win alone.

memorableLines.text: Stimulation is not the same as culture.
memorableLines.why: It warns against mistaking energy for trust.
It keeps the chapter grounded and avoids pop-neuroscience overreach.

memorableLines.text: A group can be highly motivated and still become less trustworthy.
memorableLines.why: It states the chapter's central paradox in plain words.
